<reason>PRO opened strongly with the three-element test, the casino design toolkit, and a memorable scratch-card framing, and later landed a real hit with "money or money's worth" using CON's own skin-site concession. But CON did the sharper analytical work across the debate: it showed PRO's operative criterion drifting from stake-chance-prize to friction/delivery to tiers/near-miss reels once Pokémon cards were excused, and argued convincingly that every criterion PRO reached for is a design variable consumer law can mandate universally. The decisive exchange was on verification: PRO's answer that the gate is a platform account's "stated age" was exposed by CON as either the checkbox that changes nothing or real identity verification for every paying player—a dilemma PRO's closing never resolved, and one that PRO's own opening (a child spending his mother's card) quietly undercuts. CON answered both pressure questions directly with A1/A2, honestly conceding CS:GO-style tradeable crates while explaining why a universal motion can't borrow from that minority, and rebutted PRO's "consumer law is only after-the-fact" claim. PRO's closing "burden shift" and "you built the scaffolding, you concede the harm" were rhetorically effective, but CON's "the harm is the wrapper, not the contents" answered them. CON is docked for two clipped turns and for its cash-out definition being partly neutralized, keeping the margin clear but competitive.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A4.1–A4.2 answering B3.1 while turning B4.1: CON showed its protections are universal defaults needing no age sorting, then trapped PRO's "stated age" gate between meaningless self-declaration and full gambling-grade identity verification—the cost PRO had denied throughout. PRO's closing restated burden-shift language without escaping the dilemma.</best_rebuttal>
